high-crp-what-it-means.name: High CRP: what it means and what happens next
high-crp-what-it-means.summary: A high CRP means there is inflammation or infection somewhere in the body, but not where or why, so doctors read it with symptoms and other tests.
keyPoints: A high CRP shows that inflammation or infection is likely, but it does not show where it is or what is causing it.
CRP is a protein made by the liver that rises after tissue injury, infection or other inflammation.
Doctors read the result together with symptoms, an examination and other tests, and often repeat it to see which way it is going.
A high CRP can have causes that are not diseases, such as later pregnancy, the contraceptive pill or hormone replacement therapy.
The laboratory report shows the reference range used, and ranges differ between laboratories.

body.heading: What does a CRP test measure?
body.body:
CRP stands for C-reactive protein, a protein that the liver makes. Its level in the blood rises when there is inflammation somewhere in the body. Tissue injury, infection and other kinds of inflammation can all push the level up.

Doctors usually request the test when they suspect an infection or inflammation, for example after surgery. It is also used to help assess long-term inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and lupus. The sample is taken from a vein, and the sources list no special preparation.

body.heading: What does a high CRP mean?
body.body:
A high or rising CRP suggests that there is an acute infection or inflammation. It does not show where the inflammation is or which condition is causing it. For that reason the test is not diagnostic on its own. Lab Tests Online UK adds that CRP is not specific for bacterial infection and is raised in many other conditions as well.

A small rise is hard to interpret by itself, so doctors consider it alongside the whole clinical picture. In someone who already has a long-term inflammatory condition, a high level can point to a flare-up or to treatment that is not working. The cause of a high CRP cannot always be found.

body.heading: Which conditions can raise CRP?
body.body: MedlinePlus lists cancer, heart attack, infection, inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and related diseases, and rheumatic fever among the conditions that can raise CRP. Not every cause is an illness. CRP can be higher in the later stages of pregnancy, in women who use the contraceptive pill and in women who take hormone replacement therapy. Lab Tests Online UK also links obesity with higher levels. StatPearls describes smoking, diabetes and other long-term conditions as associated with low-grade inflammation that can raise CRP.

body.heading: What happens after a high CRP result?
body.body:
The doctor reads the result alongside signs and symptoms, a physical examination and other tests. That can help show whether someone has an acute inflammatory condition or a flare-up of a long-term one. The doctor may then arrange further tests or treatment.

The test is often repeated to follow progress, because CRP falls as inflammation settles. A falling level suggests that the inflammation is easing. Lab Tests Online UK says results from a test requested by a GP take about seven working days on average to come back from the hospital. A CRP result does not say how urgent an illness is, so severe symptoms such as sudden chest pain or collapse need a 999 call, and feeling more and more unwell needs NHS 111 or the GP the same day.

body.heading: Is hs-CRP the same test?
body.body: High-sensitivity CRP, or hs-CRP, is a separate and more sensitive version of the test. It has been used to estimate the risk of heart disease in people who seem healthy. Lab Tests Online UK notes that current UK guidelines on cardiovascular risk assessment do not recommend hs-CRP testing.

body.heading: Can medicines or other factors change the result?
body.body: StatPearls states that some medicines, including non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and statins, can lower CRP. Long-term conditions linked with low-grade inflammation can lift it. Because of these influences, a single value is rarely read on its own.

body.heading: Where else is CRP used?
body.body: Regional NHS guidance on suspected giant cell arteritis, an inflammation of blood vessels, asks for a CRP before steroids are started. NHS 111 Wales says that if both ESR and CRP are normal, it is unlikely that polymyalgia rheumatica will be diagnosed. During follow-up of polymyalgia rheumatica, blood tests can check the level of inflammation in the body. NHS Tayside referral guidance asks for a CRP and an anti-CCP antibody test, with hand and foot X-rays, when rheumatoid arthritis is suspected. It advises referral for persistent symptoms even when CRP is normal and antibodies are negative. Lab Tests Online UK adds that CRP is used to monitor people after surgery or other invasive procedures for signs of infection during recovery.

references.title: Lab Tests Online UK: C-reactive protein (CRP)
StatPearls: C-reactive protein, clinical relevance and interpretation

low-ferritin-what-it-means.name: Low ferritin: what it means and what next
low-ferritin-what-it-means.summary: A low ferritin level means the body's iron stores are low, and doctors then look for the cause, which is often blood loss.
keyPoints: Ferritin is a protein that stores iron, so a low level means there is not much iron in store.
Ferritin can fall before blood iron levels fall, which makes it the most sensitive early marker of iron deficiency.
Iron deficiency is often caused by blood loss or pregnancy, so doctors look for the source.
Inflammation, infection and liver disease can raise ferritin, so it is often read alongside CRP.
The report shows the reference range used by the laboratory, which differs between laboratories.

body.heading: What does a ferritin test measure?
body.body: Ferritin is a protein that stores iron in the body. The test estimates how much iron is held in store. Doctors order it when they suspect the body has too little or too much iron, and it is most often requested for suspected low iron. Lab Tests Online UK calls it the most sensitive early marker of iron deficiency.

body.heading: What does a low ferritin level mean?
body.body: A low ferritin points to iron deficiency. The NHS explains that when ferritin is low, there is not much iron stored in the body. Stores can drop well below normal before the iron level in the blood itself falls, so ferritin can show the problem early. Low iron can exist without anaemia, and symptoms such as tiredness can still be present. Ferritin can also fall when protein levels are very low, as in some cases of malnutrition.

body.heading: Why do iron stores run low?
body.body: The NHS says iron deficiency anaemia is caused by a lack of iron, often because of blood loss or pregnancy. NHS formulary guidance lists heavy periods, bleeding in the digestive tract, coeliac disease and a poor diet among the causes. It also lists ulcers, medicines such as aspirin and anti-inflammatory painkillers, and bowel cancer as possible digestive causes, which is why the cause is looked for. Guidance for NHS Scotland says a low ferritin should be investigated for causes such as coeliac disease.

body.heading: What symptoms go with low iron?
body.body: The NHS lists tiredness, shortness of breath, noticeable heartbeats and pale skin as common symptoms. Less common symptoms include hair loss, ringing in the ears, itchy skin, a sore tongue and a craving for non-food items. That craving, called pica, can be for items such as ice, paper or clay. The NHS advises seeing a GP when symptoms like these appear, and a GP appointment is the usual route for a ferritin test.

body.heading: Why can a ferritin result be misleading?
body.body: Ferritin is not only a store of iron. Lab Tests Online UK says levels can be high in inflammatory conditions, infection and liver disease. Because inflammation can push ferritin up and hide a shortage of iron, CRP is often checked alongside it. A high ferritin can signal long-term iron overload, especially haemochromatosis, but further investigation is needed before that diagnosis is made.

body.heading: What happens next?
body.body: A GP usually takes a blood test, and ferritin is the key marker of how much iron is stored. If the cause is not clear, the GP may arrange further tests to find the source. Once the cause has been found, such as an ulcer or heavy periods, the GP recommends treatment for it. Iron tablets are the usual first treatment, and the NHS says they are taken for about six months. Side effects of iron tablets, mainly in the digestive system, are common. Iron can also be given by infusion into a vein, which is used less often. Repeat blood tests over the following months check that the iron level is returning to normal.

body.heading: What helps iron stores recover?
body.body: The NHS says iron deficiency anaemia is treated with iron tablets and with iron-rich foods. NHS guidance points to dark green leafy vegetables and dried fruit as food sources. Formulary guidance also lists iron-fortified bread, meat, apricots, prunes and raisins. NHS guidance says drinking orange juice after an iron tablet may help the body absorb the iron. Tea, coffee, milk and dairy foods, and wholegrain cereals can stop the body absorbing iron from other foods and tablets. NHS 111 Wales says iron tablets taken with or soon after food can reduce side effects, and that tablets should be continued even if side effects occur. Somerset formulary guidance adds that treatment continues for some months after the iron level is corrected, so that stores can be replenished. Tablets can cause constipation or diarrhoea, tummy pain, heartburn, nausea and darker stools.

body.heading: What about pregnancy?
body.body: A Scottish maternity guideline states that iron requirements are higher in pregnancy than in women who menstruate. It recommends that women who start oral iron continue it through pregnancy and for some months after the birth.

references.title: Lab Tests Online UK: Ferritin test

cholesterol-blood-test-results-explained.name: Cholesterol test results explained
cholesterol-blood-test-results-explained.summary: A cholesterol test reports total, HDL and non-HDL cholesterol plus triglycerides, and doctors read them with other risk factors.
keyPoints: A standard cholesterol test reports total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol and non-HDL cholesterol, and triglycerides are usually measured with them.
Non-HDL cholesterol is total cholesterol minus HDL, and it covers all the harmful types together.
Doctors use cholesterol results with age, blood pressure and health conditions to estimate the risk of cardiovascular disease.
Where treatment is needed, guidance recommends lifestyle support and often a statin, with the test repeated afterwards.

body.heading: What does a cholesterol blood test measure?
body.body: A lipid profile measures lipids in the blood, such as cholesterol and triglycerides. The sample is taken from a vein in the arm, sometimes after fasting. A standard test reports total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol and non-HDL cholesterol, and triglycerides are usually measured alongside them. LDL cholesterol is tested less routinely, and doctors order it when the healthcare team thinks treatment may be needed.

body.heading: What do HDL, non-HDL and triglycerides mean?
body.body: HDL is generally treated as the protective part of the total, and a low HDL counts as a risk marker. Non-HDL cholesterol is total cholesterol minus HDL. It adds up the harmful types of cholesterol, so it can be more informative than LDL alone. Lab Tests Online UK notes that non-HDL does not need a fasting sample, which makes it practical. Triglycerides are a type of fat in the blood. Fasting is needed only for some triglyceride tests, because fasting triglycerides are more accurate and are done if the non-fasting result is high.

body.heading: Which numbers count as healthy?
body.body: The NHS lists target levels for healthy adults and stricter goals after a heart attack or stroke. Sources differ slightly on where they place the line for triglycerides, and laboratories differ in their reference ranges. For that reason the laboratory report shows the range used for each result.

body.heading: How does a doctor use the result?
body.body: Doctors use the cholesterol result with age, blood pressure and health conditions to estimate the risk of cardiovascular disease. The QRISK tool estimates cardiovascular risk and helps decide whether treatment is needed. For people who already have cardiovascular disease, the pathways skip QRISK because their risk is already high. A GP or practice nurse takes the sample, and a finger-prick test may be offered in some pharmacies or at an NHS Health Check in England.

body.heading: What helps lower raised cholesterol?
body.body: NHS pathways encourage a diet rich in fruit, vegetables and wholegrains and low in saturated fat. They also encourage regular moderate aerobic activity. In primary prevention, lifestyle support is given for a few months before the level is reassessed. Where treatment is needed, the pathways favour a high-intensity statin. Ezetimibe is a second-line option if the aim is not reached. Someone who has side effects on a high-intensity statin can be offered a lower dose or another statin. The test is repeated after treatment starts to see whether the level has fallen.

body.heading: Why does raised cholesterol matter?
body.body: The BHF explains that cholesterol builds up in the artery walls as fatty material called atheroma. That gradual build-up raises the risk of heart attack and stroke. Risk rises further in people who also have high blood pressure, diabetes or who smoke. Most people with high cholesterol have no symptoms.

body.heading: What is familial hypercholesterolaemia?
body.body: Familial hypercholesterolaemia is an inherited form of high cholesterol. South West London guidance describes the risk of heart attack or stroke at a younger age as especially high in this condition. The BHF lists a high result on a routine blood test, or a heart attack or stroke at a younger age, as warning signs.

body.heading: What do statins do, and who is offered them?
body.body: NHS guidance says statins may be offered to people at higher risk of cardiovascular disease when healthy lifestyle changes have not helped or are unlikely to help on their own. They are also used in people who already have heart disease and in people with inherited high cholesterol. If statins are unsuitable, other cholesterol-lowering medicines can be offered. The BHF says people usually combine healthy lifestyle choices with medicine to lower cholesterol. Essex integrated care board guidance lists a better diet, regular activity and a healthy weight as the basics.

Lab Tests Online UK: Lipid profile

hba1c-test-what-it-shows.name: HbA1c test: what it shows and why it matters
hba1c-test-what-it-shows.summary: The HbA1c test shows average blood glucose over the past two to three months and is used to diagnose and monitor diabetes.
keyPoints: HbA1c reflects the average blood glucose level over roughly the previous two to three months.
The test is used to diagnose diabetes, to check how well diabetes is managed and to follow people with prediabetes.
Targets are personal, and a diabetes team may set a higher one for someone with frequent low blood glucose or an older person.
Conditions that affect red blood cells can make HbA1c unreliable, and another test may suit better.

body.heading: What does an HbA1c test show?
body.body: The HbA1c blood test reflects the average level of glucose in the blood over the past two to three months. That is why it differs from a finger-prick reading, which captures one moment. Glucose attaches to a part of the red blood cell, and the more glucose there is in the blood, the more HbA1c is present. Red blood cells live for about two to three months before new ones replace them, which sets the window the test covers. Occasional very high or very low readings are smoothed into one average.

body.heading: What is the test used for?
body.body: Doctors use it to diagnose diabetes. They also use it to keep an eye on levels in people at risk of developing diabetes, a state called prediabetes. In people who already have diabetes, it shows how well blood sugar has been controlled. MedlinePlus says the test is not used to diagnose type 1 diabetes. Home glucose monitors do not diagnose diabetes, and diagnosis rests on blood tests that a GP arranges.

body.heading: How are the results given and what are the targets?
body.body: UK laboratories give HbA1c in millimoles per mole, while some countries use a percentage. Diabetes UK says targets are individual and each person agrees their own with their diabetes care team. A higher target may suit someone who has had many problems with low blood glucose. As people age, the diabetes team may raise the target, because the risks of tight control can outweigh the benefits.

body.heading: How often is it done?
body.body: Diabetes UK says HbA1c is usually tested every three to six months in people with diabetes. It may be done more often when blood glucose is changing quickly, when planning a pregnancy or after a change of treatment. Some people need the test less often, usually later in pregnancy.

body.heading: What can make the result less reliable?
body.body: Conditions that affect red blood cells can make the result less accurate, such as anaemia or an uncommon form of haemoglobin. Diabetes UK advises talking to the doctor about which other test will be more accurate in that case. Pregnancy or illness during the window can also affect the result. An NHS Scotland resource says the HbA1c may change if diet, physical activity, weight or medication have changed. Laboratories often convert the result to an estimated average glucose, which may differ from readings on a home meter.

body.heading: What happens after a result in the prediabetes range?
body.body: Scottish NHS guidance says the GP should explain the risk factors for type 2 diabetes and what changes can reduce the risk. Diabetes UK says the GP should refer people to a free NHS type 2 diabetes prevention course. A blood test to check average blood sugar should be offered at least once a year. A GP appointment is the route to discuss any result.

body.heading: Why does a prediabetes result matter?
body.body: Prediabetes means blood sugar is higher than normal but not high enough for a diagnosis of type 2 diabetes. It also means a high risk of developing type 2 diabetes. Prediabetes usually causes no symptoms, so it is often found only through a routine blood test or an NHS Health Check. Feeling very thirsty, passing urine more often, feeling more tired than usual and losing weight without trying are symptoms of diabetes itself. Anyone with those symptoms is advised to speak to a GP. The NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme is a free programme for people at risk of type 2 diabetes, with support on eating, weight and activity, and a doctor or nurse makes the referral.

liver-function-tests-what-results-mean.name: Liver blood tests: what the results mean
liver-function-tests-what-results-mean.summary: Liver blood tests point towards a possible problem but cannot name the cause, and abnormal results are common and often not serious.
keyPoints: Liver blood tests, once called liver function tests, are a group of tests that include ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, bilirubin and albumin.
A result outside the reference range does not always mean liver disease, and a normal result does not always rule it out.
The pattern of results helps point towards liver cell injury or a problem with bile flow.
Yellowing of the skin or eyes needs an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111, according to the NHS.

body.heading: What are liver blood tests?
body.body: Liver blood tests are a group of blood tests, once known as liver function tests or LFTs. They usually include ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, bilirubin and albumin. They are often done as routine tests, so abnormal results are sometimes found by chance when blood is taken for another reason.

body.heading: What do ALT and AST show?
body.body: ALT and AST are enzymes that leak into the blood when liver cells are injured. ALT is more specific to the liver, while AST can also be high when muscle is damaged elsewhere in the body. Common causes of this pattern include viral hepatitis, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, alcohol-related liver disease, autoimmune hepatitis and drug-induced liver injury.

body.heading: What do ALP, GGT, bilirubin and albumin show?
body.body: Raised ALP and GGT point towards a problem with the flow of bile. Causes include blocked bile ducts, for example by stones, and some long-term diseases of the bile ducts. ALP also comes from bone, so GGT helps to show whether the liver is the source. Raised bilirubin causes jaundice, a yellowing of the eyes and skin. Bilirubin can also be raised without liver disease, as in Gilbert's syndrome, where the other liver tests are normal. Albumin is affected only when liver disease is at a severe stage, and low albumin also has other causes such as malnutrition, kidney protein loss and inflammation.

body.heading: Does an abnormal result mean liver disease?
body.body: Abnormal results can occur in conditions that do not involve the liver, and normal results can be found in people with serious liver disease. The British Liver Trust says it is quite common to get a result that is not normal, and this does not always mean a liver condition. It adds that the liver can take a lot of damage before it causes problems, so a normal result is a good sign but not a guarantee. Illness, shock, burns, injury, severe exercise, pregnancy and a reaction to medicines can all change one or more of the tests. Sometimes a repeat test is all that is needed.

body.heading: What happens after an abnormal result?
body.body: Laboratories compare each result with their own range, so results are compared only with the range of the laboratory that did the test. If the results suggest a liver problem, a GP may calculate a FIB-4 index, which gives an indication of the amount of scarring in the liver. People at high risk of liver disease, or with symptoms, are referred or have more tests. Further tests can look for the cause, such as viral hepatitis, fatty liver disease or an effect of alcohol or medicines.

body.heading: When is yellowing of the skin urgent?
body.body: The NHS says jaundice can be a sign of something serious such as liver disease. It advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or contacting NHS 111 when the skin or whites of the eyes look yellow. On brown or black skin the yellow colour is easier to see in the whites of the eyes. Itchy skin, darker urine and paler stools can come with it.

body.heading: What are fatty liver and alcohol-related liver disease?
body.body: NHS guidance names non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, in some pathways now called MASLD, as a common cause of abnormal liver tests. NHS inform says the mainstay of care for non-alcoholic fatty liver disease is lifestyle advice to reduce weight and increase physical activity. It adds that there is currently no specific medicine for it. Where alcohol is the cause, one pathway advises cutting out alcohol and repeating the test after a month. Local guidance suggests repeating the tests after reviewing medicines or a recent illness before moving on to scans. If results stay abnormal, guidance supports an ultrasound scan of the liver and bile ducts and blood tests for viral and autoimmune causes. A standard ultrasound does not assess scarring, so another scan may be needed. Jaundice, weight loss, a swollen abdomen, confusion, bleeding or a low albumin warrant urgent referral, according to local NHS guidance.

references.title: British Liver Trust: Liver blood tests
Lab Tests Online UK: Liver blood tests
MyHealth Devon (NHS): Abnormal liver blood tests

egfr-and-creatinine-kidney-blood-tests.name: eGFR and creatinine: kidney test results
egfr-and-creatinine-kidney-blood-tests.summary: Creatinine and eGFR show how well the kidneys filter blood, and kidney disease is confirmed only when abnormal results persist.
keyPoints: Creatinine is a waste product measured in the blood, and eGFR is an estimate of kidney filtering worked out from it.
As kidney function worsens, creatinine goes up and eGFR goes down.
One abnormal result is not enough to diagnose chronic kidney disease, which is confirmed when eGFR stays low over about three months.
A urine test, the albumin to creatinine ratio, is used alongside eGFR because it can show kidney damage.

body.heading: What are creatinine and eGFR?
body.body: Creatinine is a waste product, and the blood test measures how much of it is in the blood. The eGFR, or estimated glomerular filtration rate, is calculated from the creatinine result. The calculation also takes account of age and sex. Lab Tests Online UK explains that as kidney function worsens, creatinine goes up and the eGFR goes down. Because eGFR comes from a routine blood test, it lets clinicians spot kidney problems before symptoms appear.

body.heading: What does a low eGFR mean?
body.body: A low eGFR means the kidneys are filtering less well than expected. The National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases treats a reduced eGFR as one sign of decreased kidney function. The other key sign is kidney damage, usually shown by albumin, a protein, in the urine. eGFR falls naturally with age, which does not always mean kidney disease. The estimate is unreliable when kidney function is changing quickly, as in acute kidney injury.

body.heading: How is chronic kidney disease confirmed?
body.body: One abnormal result is not enough. A diagnosis is usually confirmed only if repeated eGFR tests are consistently lower than normal over about three months. A primary care study warned that relying on a single test could overestimate how many people have chronic kidney disease. The urine albumin to creatinine ratio, or ACR, compares albumin with creatinine in a urine sample. Alongside the eGFR, urine tests give a more accurate picture of how well the kidneys are working. Results are classed by eGFR category and by ACR category, which together show the stage.

body.heading: Who is tested?
body.body: Testing is recommended for people with risk factors such as diabetes, high blood pressure, past acute kidney injury or cardiovascular disease. Early chronic kidney disease often causes no symptoms, so it is commonly found through routine blood or urine tests. Later symptoms can include tiredness, swollen ankles, feet or hands, shortness of breath, blood in the urine and passing urine more often at night. The NHS advises seeing a GP about symptoms that persist.

body.heading: What are the limits of the test?
body.body: Creatinine-based eGFR may be less reliable in older adults. In that situation another marker, cystatin C, can help. Creatinine can also be influenced by factors other than the kidneys, so the report shows the reference range used.

body.heading: What happens after a diagnosis?
body.body: Chronic kidney disease is most often caused by damage from other conditions, most commonly diabetes and high blood pressure. There is no cure, but care can slow progression. Kidney function is monitored with regular blood and urine tests. Care centres on blood pressure control, managing diabetes, prescribed medicines, diet advice and not smoking. If chronic kidney disease advances, a referral to a kidney specialist may follow.

body.heading: How often are kidney tests repeated?
body.body: NICE guideline NG203 says the monitoring frequency it recommends is a minimum, and that more frequent monitoring may suit some people. The frequency is agreed between the person and their healthcare professional. It also reflects how quickly the eGFR or ACR is changing and other conditions such as diabetes. NICE says ACR monitoring should be individualised, for example more often when the ACR is higher. NICE lists diabetes among the risk factors for which eGFR and ACR testing is advised.

high-white-blood-cell-count-causes.name: High white blood cell count: what it means
high-white-blood-cell-count-causes.summary: A high white blood cell count is a non-specific sign, most often from infection, and doctors read it with the type of cell raised.
keyPoints: A high white cell count can be caused by infection, inflammation, some medicines, stress or smoking, and less often by a blood disorder.
The differential count shows which type of white cell is raised, which helps narrow down the cause.
A mild, lasting rise is often linked to chronic inflammation, infection or smoking, while an unexplained very high count leads to urgent referral to haematology.
A single high count does not diagnose anything, and doctors may repeat the test.

body.heading: What does the full blood count measure?
body.body: NHS inform says a full blood count checks the types and numbers of cells in the blood, including red cells, white cells and platelets. The test gives a total white cell count and a differential that splits white cells into types. Those types include neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils. Neutrophils are the main defence against bacterial infection.

body.heading: What does a high white cell count mean?
body.body: A raised count is a non-specific signal, which means it does not point to one cause. A high count can indicate infection, inflammation, or leukaemia and other blood disorders. Infection, most often bacterial infection, is the most common cause. Results vary with age and time of day, and older people sometimes do not show a raised count even when they have an infection.

body.heading: What else can raise it?
body.body: Inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis can raise the count, and so can allergies. Some medicines, for example corticosteroids, can raise it. Tissue damage such as burns can raise it. Severe physical or emotional stress, for example from an injury or surgery, can raise it. Smoking and pregnancy can also raise the count.

body.heading: What does the differential add?
body.body: A high neutrophil count usually suggests bacterial infection, inflammation or physical stress on the body. A high lymphocyte count can occur with viral infections or with conditions such as chronic lymphocytic leukaemia. Leukaemia and Hodgkin disease can cause persistently high counts, which is why doctors follow up unexplained rises.

body.heading: What happens next?
body.body: A hospital guideline from Hampshire says a mild, lasting rise is likely to come from a chronic inflammatory or infective process, or from smoking. The same guideline says an unexplained, very high count prompts an urgent referral to haematology. Doctors read the count with symptoms, the differential and sometimes a repeat test or a blood film. Reference ranges differ with age, sex and laboratory, so the report shows the range used. Feeling unwell with a fever is a reason to contact NHS 111 or the GP the same day, and severe breathing difficulty or collapse needs a 999 call.

body.heading: When might a blood disorder be considered?
body.body: A GP may order a blood test if leukaemia is suspected, and a very high number of abnormal white cells can point towards it. In that case the person is referred urgently to a specialist in blood conditions, called a haematologist. Symptoms listed by the NHS across leukaemia types include tiredness, bleeding or bruising easily, night sweats, weight loss and frequent infections. The NHS stresses that having these symptoms does not mean someone has leukaemia, and that many are caused by more common conditions. For chronic myeloid leukaemia the NHS advises a non-urgent GP visit if symptoms appear.

references.title: Lab Tests Online UK: White blood cell count
Lab Tests Online UK: Full blood count

thyroid-blood-tests-tsh-and-t4-explained.name: Thyroid blood tests: TSH and T4 explained
thyroid-blood-tests-tsh-and-t4-explained.summary: Thyroid tests read TSH and free T4 together: a high TSH with low T4 suggests an underactive thyroid, and the reverse an overactive one.
keyPoints: TSH is the most sensitive marker of thyroid status, and it is read together with free T4.
A high TSH with a low free T4 suggests an underactive thyroid, and a low TSH with a high free T4 suggests an overactive thyroid.
A slightly raised TSH with a normal free T4 is called subclinical hypothyroidism and is followed over time.
Severe illness and some medicines can change thyroid results without a thyroid disease.

body.heading: What do TSH and T4 show?
body.body: The thyroid is a gland in the neck that makes thyroid hormones. Thyroid-stimulating hormone, or TSH, comes from the pituitary gland and tells the thyroid how much hormone to make. The British Thyroid Foundation calls TSH the most sensitive marker of thyroid status. T4 is the main thyroid hormone, and doctors usually look at free T4, the part not bound to proteins. Results are read as a pattern of TSH and free T4 together, not one number alone.

body.heading: What pattern suggests an underactive thyroid?
body.body: A high TSH with a low free T4 suggests an underactive thyroid, called hypothyroidism. The NHS says a blood test measuring hormone levels is the only accurate way to find out whether there is a problem. A GP will also ask about symptoms and may examine the neck. Thyroid UK says a low free T4 with a raised TSH will usually give a diagnosis of hypothyroidism.

body.heading: What pattern suggests an overactive thyroid?
body.body: The reverse pattern, a low TSH with a high free T4, suggests an overactive thyroid, called hyperthyroidism. The NHS describes blood tests as part of how an overactive thyroid is diagnosed.

body.heading: What if the results are borderline?
body.body: A slightly raised TSH with a normal free T4 is called subclinical hypothyroidism. It may gradually develop into clinical hypothyroidism over many years. A test for thyroid antibodies helps to judge that risk. Thyroid UK says there is no evidence that routine early treatment helps when the TSH is only a little above the reference range. A low TSH with a low free T4 may come from a problem with the pituitary gland, or from a significant illness that does not involve the thyroid.

body.heading: Can illness or medicines change the result?
body.body: Abnormal T4 levels do not always mean a condition that needs treatment. Severe illness and some medicines, such as birth control pills and steroids, can affect T4 levels.

body.heading: What happens after a diagnosis?
body.body: Underactive thyroid is usually treated with daily hormone replacement tablets called levothyroxine. The NHS says this treatment is long term to prevent symptoms. NHS inform says a mild case with no symptoms may not need treatment. Regular blood tests check that the dose is right, because a wrong dose can cause side effects such as feeling sick, diarrhoea, headaches or problems sleeping. For people on replacement, TSH is the main test used to check that the treatment is adequate.

body.heading: What can cause an underactive or overactive thyroid?
body.body: In the UK the main cause of an underactive thyroid is an autoimmune condition called Hashimoto's disease. Damage to the thyroid during treatment for an overactive thyroid or thyroid cancer is another cause. Common symptoms of an underactive thyroid include tiredness, weight gain, feeling cold, constipation and low mood, and they develop slowly. Graves' disease is the most common cause of an overactive thyroid. Symptoms of an overactive thyroid include nervousness, weight loss despite a good appetite, a fast or irregular heartbeat, tremor and sleep difficulty. Treatment for an overactive thyroid can include anti-thyroid medicines, beta-blockers for symptoms such as tremor, and radioactive iodine. Radioactive iodine often leads to an underactive thyroid afterwards. In Graves' disease, blood tests look for antibodies as well as hormone levels.

vitamin-b12-and-folate-tests-explained.name: Vitamin B12 and folate tests explained
vitamin-b12-and-folate-tests-explained.summary: B12 and folate blood tests help find the cause of deficiency anaemia, but a B12 result alone can miss cases, so symptoms matter too.
keyPoints: Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency can both cause anaemia in which the body makes abnormally large red blood cells.
A GP combines symptoms with blood tests that check the level of vitamin B12 and of folate.
A UK clinical guideline says a B12 blood test is not completely reliable, so two tests are requested when deficiency is suspected.
B12 deficiency is usually treated with injections of hydroxocobalamin, and folate deficiency with folic acid tablets.

body.heading: What are vitamin B12 and folate deficiency anaemia?
body.body: Vitamin B12 and folate are both needed to make healthy red blood cells. When either is lacking, the body can make abnormally large red blood cells that do not work as they should. This is called vitamin B12 or folate deficiency anaemia.

body.heading: What symptoms can it cause?
body.body: The NHS lists tiredness along with numbness, muscle weakness, psychological problems, problems with balance and coordination, pins and needles and incontinence. Folate deficiency anaemia adds symptoms such as breathlessness, pale skin and palpitations. Some effects of B12 deficiency can appear without anaemia and without a low blood level. Mouth ulcers, a sore red tongue and problems with vision or memory are also listed.

body.heading: How is it diagnosed?
body.body: A GP typically combines symptoms with blood tests. The blood tests check the level of vitamin B12 and the level of folate in the blood. A UK clinical guideline notes that a vitamin B12 blood test is not completely reliable and asks for two tests when deficiency is suspected. The same guideline says routine screening for B12 deficiency is not appropriate. The NHS says a GP should be involved when the cause is unclear, in pregnancy, or when symptoms suggest the nervous system is affected.

body.heading: What causes deficiency?
body.body: The NHS says pernicious anaemia is the most common cause of vitamin B12 deficiency in the UK. Pernicious anaemia is an autoimmune condition that affects the stomach, so B12 from food is not absorbed. Lack of B12 from the diet is uncommon, but it can happen with a vegan diet that includes no supplements or fortified foods. Some medicines, including proton pump inhibitors and metformin, can reduce B12 levels. Folate deficiency can be linked to some medicines, such as certain anticonvulsants and methotrexate.

body.heading: How is it treated?
body.body: B12 deficiency anaemia is usually treated with injections of vitamin B12, called hydroxocobalamin. When the cause is diet, treatment may be daily B12 tablets instead. Folate deficiency is usually treated with folic acid tablets. Clinicians check B12 status first, because folic acid can mask a vitamin B12 deficiency. Follow-up blood tests check that treatment is working. A GP appointment is the route for symptoms such as numbness, pins and needles or problems with balance.

vitamin-d-blood-test-who-needs-one.name: Vitamin D blood test: who needs one?
vitamin-d-blood-test-who-needs-one.summary: NHS guidance does not recommend routine vitamin D tests for people without symptoms, and testing is kept for specific symptoms or conditions.
keyPoints: NHS guidance says not to test routinely for vitamin D deficiency in people without symptoms.
Testing is considered for bone pain, muscle weakness, abnormal calcium results, malabsorption or kidney disease.
A lack of vitamin D can cause rickets in children and bone pain from osteomalacia in adults.
The NHS says everyone can consider a daily supplement in autumn and winter, and people at higher risk all year.

body.heading: What does a vitamin D blood test show?
body.body: The test measures the level of vitamin D in the blood, usually as 25-hydroxyvitamin D. The body makes vitamin D under the skin when it is exposed to sunlight. In the UK, levels tend to drop in winter.

body.heading: Who is tested and who is not?
body.body: NHS guidance says not to test routinely for vitamin D deficiency in people without symptoms. Testing is generally considered for bone pain or softness in adults, a condition called osteomalacia, and for unexplained muscle weakness. It is also considered for abnormal calcium or parathyroid hormone results, before some bone treatments, and in malabsorption conditions and kidney disease. People at higher risk who have no symptoms do not need routine testing but should be advised on a maintenance supplement. Higher risk applies to people over a certain age, those who get little sun and those with darker skin.

body.heading: What does a low level cause?
body.body: A lack of vitamin D can lead to bone deformities such as rickets in children. In adults it can cause bone pain through osteomalacia. An NHS medical director described more general signs of tiredness and aches and pains. In some cases the bones can become softer.

body.heading: How are the results read?
body.body: One NHS trust laboratory divides results into deficient, possibly inadequate for some people, and sufficient for almost everyone. A level in the middle band may be adequate in some people, yet treatment is advised when someone has the symptoms that prompted the test. Local guidance varies, so the report shows the range used by the laboratory. Treatment for confirmed deficiency is usually set by a clinician.

body.heading: Who is advised to take a supplement?
body.body: NHS England advice is that everyone should consider taking a daily vitamin D supplement during the autumn and winter. Scottish advice is similar and applies from age five upwards. People at higher risk are advised to take a supplement all year, including pregnant and breastfeeding women, children under five, and people with little sun exposure. People of African, African-Caribbean and South Asian origin are also in the higher-risk group. NHS guidance warns that taking too much vitamin D could be harmful. Most people buy standard supplements over the counter, because NHS England has moved away from routine prescribing for prevention.

body.heading: Where else does vitamin D come from?
body.body: Sunlight on the skin is the main source in the warmer months. Food sources include oily fish, egg yolks and fortified foods.

body.heading: What are rickets and osteomalacia?
body.body: Low vitamin D often causes no symptoms. Some people have symptoms such as tiredness and aches. In children, a deficiency can lead to rickets, where the bones are weak, soft and can become deformed. Rickets is more common in children with darker skin who spend little time in the sun. Local NHS guidance lists premature babies, exclusively breastfed babies and children taking some anticonvulsants as other higher-risk groups.

troponin-blood-test-what-it-shows.name: Troponin blood test: what it shows
troponin-blood-test-what-it-shows.summary: A troponin test measures proteins released when heart muscle is damaged, and a raised result does not always mean a heart attack.
keyPoints: Troponin T and troponin I are proteins released into the blood when heart muscle is damaged.
The more damage, the more troponin reaches the blood, and levels rise over hours, so the test is often repeated.
A raised troponin may point to a heart attack, but other conditions can raise it too.
The NHS says to call 999 for chest pain that is tight or squeezing, or that spreads to the arms, neck or jaw.

body.heading: What is troponin?
body.body: Troponin T and troponin I are proteins found in heart muscle. They are released into the blood when the heart muscle is damaged, for example in a heart attack. The more damage there is, the more troponin reaches the blood.

body.heading: Why is a troponin test done?
body.body: Clinicians mainly use the test to check whether a heart attack is happening or has recently happened. It is typically ordered when someone has chest pain or other signs of a heart attack. It can also be ordered for worsening angina without other signs of a heart attack, and to look for other causes of heart injury.

body.heading: How is it used in hospital?
body.body: The NHS treats an ECG as an important early test in a suspected heart attack, and says it should be done within 10 minutes of arrival at hospital. Blood tests look for troponin, which leaks slowly into the blood after damage to the heart. Levels usually rise over hours, so testing is often repeated over several hours. NICE guidance quoted by the NHS says a second troponin sample is usually taken a few hours after the first, unless the first is normal and the risk is judged low. Newer high-sensitivity tests can detect a rise sooner after chest pain begins.

body.heading: What does a normal or raised result mean?
body.body: Normal levels some hours after symptoms began make a heart attack unlikely. Very high levels most often mean a heart attack has occurred. Raised levels do not always mean a heart attack, because other heart conditions can raise troponin. A UK study reported by University Hospital Southampton found raised troponin in some people with unrelated conditions, so results need careful interpretation. After a heart attack, levels may stay high for one to two weeks.

body.heading: How do the results fit with the ECG?
body.body: The ECG and troponin results together help to identify the type of heart attack. A STEMI shows particular changes on the ECG. An NSTEMI is found when the ECG does not show those changes but blood tests show heart damage.

body.heading: When is chest pain an emergency?
body.body: The NHS advises calling 999 for chest pain that feels tight or squeezing, or that spreads to the arms, neck or jaw. Severe difficulty breathing, pale, blue or grey lips or skin, and passing out also need a 999 call. The NHS says not to drive to A&E, because the person on the 999 line gives advice on what to do.

body.heading: What do NICE recommendations say about newer tests?
body.body: NICE recommends high-sensitivity troponin tests as options for ruling out a type of heart attack called NSTEMI in emergency departments. The approach can use a single sample on arrival, or a second sample about three hours later. NICE advises that a negative result should not lead to discharge without further investigation if the person looks visibly unwell or the sample was taken too early after the suspected event. NICE says sex-specific thresholds should be used for diagnosing a heart attack in men and women.

inr-blood-test-warfarin-explained.name: INR blood test and warfarin explained
inr-blood-test-warfarin-explained.summary: The INR blood test shows how long blood takes to clot, and it is how the effect of warfarin is monitored so the dose can be adjusted.
keyPoints: The INR measures how long the blood takes to clot, and it is the main way warfarin treatment is monitored.
Warfarin has no fixed dose, so the dose is adjusted from INR results by an anticoagulation clinic.
New medicines, alcohol and diet can change the INR.
The main side effect of warfarin is bleeding, and the NHS says to call NHS 111 for symptoms of bleeding, and 999 for bleeding that will not stop.

body.heading: What does the INR measure?
body.body: INR stands for international normalised ratio. It is a standard blood test that measures how long the blood takes to clot. One NHS trust explains that it compares the clotting time of a person taking warfarin with that of someone who is not.

body.heading: Why is the INR checked on warfarin?
body.body: Warfarin does not have a fixed dose. The dose needed depends on how much the medicine slows the clotting of the blood, and the INR test measures that effect. The main side effect of warfarin is an increased risk of bleeding, and the risk is highest when the INR is too high.

body.heading: How often is it done?
body.body: At the start, testing is frequent. Once the result is stable, the gaps between tests lengthen. Some people need tests more regularly than others. The INR results go to the warfarin clinic, which advises on the ongoing dose and the date of the next test.

body.heading: What can change the INR?
body.body: New medicines can change the effect of warfarin, so one NHS service asks for an INR test soon after any new medicine is started or stopped. Alcohol, diet and other medicines can also move the result. Sources name cranberry and grapefruit juice and binge drinking as able to raise the INR. They also name ibuprofen and similar painkillers as able to increase the risk of bleeding.

body.heading: What should people know about bleeding?
body.body: Signs of bleeding include bleeding gums, blood in vomit, blood in urine or stool, and prolonged bleeding from small cuts. For women, heavier periods can be a sign. The NHS says to call NHS 111 if there are symptoms of bleeding or other serious side effects. The British Heart Foundation says to call NHS 111 or the GP when worried about bleeding, and 999 if bleeding after an injury cannot be stopped. NHS inform says to phone 999 or go to A&E when bleeding cannot be stopped, and it lists coughing or vomiting blood among the signs. A blow to the head counts as an emergency even without visible bleeding.

body.heading: What else do people on warfarin carry or watch?
body.body: People on warfarin are given an anticoagulant alert card to carry. The card lets medical staff identify that someone takes warfarin if there is an accident. Foods high in vitamin K, such as leafy green vegetables, can affect how warfarin works. Dietary advice from an NHS trust stresses eating a steady amount of such foods, because the clinic adjusts the dose to match. The NHS says the food and drink restrictions do not usually apply to the newer anticoagulants such as apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban and dabigatran.
